title: AI tools for growing insurance brokerages: the marketing team’s 2026 playbook
summary: How to improve marketing at a growing insurance brokerage: the AI tools marketing teams use, a 7-step playbook, and why the proposal is your most-read asset.
body_markdown:
The short version


- The most-read marketing asset at any brokerage is the proposal. Every prospect and every renewal client reads it at the exact moment they decide. Most marketing teams have never seen one before it goes out.
- Growth breaks consistency first. At three producers the owner reviews everything. At thirty, the brand a client sees depends on who quoted them.[CopyCat](https://www.runcopycat.com/insurance-proposal-software) fixes that at the template level for proposals, one-pagers, email summaries, and renewal comparisons.
- Build the rest of the stack one job at a time: HubSpot for CRM and automation, Agency Revolution or AgencyZoom for insurance-specific campaigns, Canva for design, Semrush for SEO and AI search, Birdeye for reviews, Circleback for client language, Descript for video, Clay for commercial prospecting.
- Measure what the agency actually earns from: proposal-to-bind rate, retention, accounts per client, and time from quote to proposal. Leads alone hide the leak.


Marketing at a five-person agency is the owner, a website, and a referral network. Marketing at a fifty-person brokerage is a real function: a marketing lead or a small team, a CRM, campaigns by line of business, producers in three offices, and a leadership team asking what all of it returns. The tools that worked at five people stop working long before fifty.


This guide is for the people running that function. It covers the AI tools worth putting in front of a growing brokerage's marketing team, a step-by-step playbook to improve insurance agency marketing, and the channel most agency marketers overlook. We make CopyCat, so our pick for client-facing documents is not independent. The other picks are based on each vendor's published product materials and how well they fit an agency's workflow.


## What changes when an insurance agency grows


Three things break, usually in this order.


- **Consistency.** Every new producer brings a proposal habit from their last agency. Within a year the brokerage sends five different-looking proposals, three renewal formats, and whatever the newest hire built in Word. Clients notice, even when they never say it.
- **Visibility.** Leadership cannot see which lines are growing, which carriers the team quotes most, or which producers convert. Marketing runs campaigns on gut feel because the data sits in a dozen inboxes.
- **Capacity.** Account managers spend hours a week retyping carrier quotes into documents. That is time not spent on the cross-sell call, the review request, or the referral ask that marketing is counting on.


AI helps with all three, but only if each tool is matched to a specific job. A general chatbot that writes blog posts does nothing for the producer who just sent a client an unbranded comparison spreadsheet.

## The marketing channel most agencies ignore: the proposal


Agency marketing teams pour hours into the website, the newsletter, and the LinkedIn calendar. Then a producer emails a prospect a proposal built from last year's Word file, with the old logo, a different font, and a premium table pasted from a carrier PDF. That document gets more attention than anything the marketing team published all quarter. The prospect reads it line by line, forwards it to their CFO, and holds it next to the competing broker's version.


That last part is the one that should worry a growing brokerage. We have watched agencies under three people win accounts against twenty-person agencies on presentation alone. A bigger agency has more markets, more expertise, and more service depth. If its proposal looks like an afterthought, none of that shows up at the moment the client chooses. Read more in our piece on[why the proposal is the close](https://www.runcopycat.com/blog/your-proposal-is-the-close) .


For a marketing team, owning the proposal means three things:


1. **One template, enforced by software.** The agency brand, section order, standard language, and disclosures live in the[proposal template](https://www.runcopycat.com/insurance-proposal-template) , so a producer cannot drift from it by accident.
2. **A follow-up kit with every proposal.** A one-page summary for the decision maker and an email summary the producer can send in one click, in the same brand as the full document.
3. **Data on what goes out.** How many proposals the team sends, for which lines and carriers, by which producers, and how that changes month to month.

## How to improve marketing for your insurance brokerage: a 7-step playbook


This is the order we would run it in a brokerage of 10 to 100 people. Each step builds on the one before it.


### 1. Audit every document a client sees


Collect the last ten proposals, renewal summaries, and quote emails your team sent, from ten different producers. Lay them side by side. Count the logos, fonts, section orders, and disclaimers. Most marketing leads who run this exercise find the brand they spent a year building barely appears in the documents that close business.


### 2. Lock the brand in the template, not in training


A brand guide in a shared drive is a suggestion. A template in the software every producer uses is a rule. Move proposal and renewal formats into a system where the brand is applied automatically, then spend your training time on the message instead of the margins.


### 3. Turn every proposal into a follow-up sequence


The proposal is not the end of the conversation. Pair it with a one-page summary the client can forward internally and an email summary that restates the recommendation. Then set a short follow-up sequence in your CRM tied to the proposal date. Most lost deals are not lost to a competitor. They go quiet.


### 4. Market to your own book first


The cheapest new premium at a growing brokerage is the account you already have. Use your AMS and proposal data to find monoline clients, commercial accounts without umbrella or cyber, and households with auto but not home. Build campaigns by line of business, and give producers the talking points before the email goes out so the follow-up call sounds the same as the campaign.


### 5. Get found in AI search, not just Google


Business owners now ask ChatGPT, Gemini, and Google's AI answers which broker to call for contractor insurance in their city. Those tools cite pages that answer the question directly. Publish plain answers to the questions your producers hear every week, by line and by industry. Keep your agency name, address, and services identical across your site, Google Business Profile, and directories. Then track how often AI answers mention you, the same way you track rankings.


### 6. Build a review engine across every office


Reviews drive local search and referral trust. Ask at the moments clients are happiest: right after a bind, a smooth renewal, or a paid claim. Automate the request, route negative feedback to a manager, and respond to every review within a day. For multi-office agencies, track each location separately so one quiet office does not hide behind a busy one.


### 7. Feed the marketing team the client's own words


The best campaign copy comes from what clients say on calls. With consent, capture producer meetings, pull out the recurring questions and objections, and send them to marketing monthly. That turns "why is my premium up" into a renewal email, a FAQ page, and a short video, all built on the language clients actually use.

## The insurance marketing metrics that matter


Leads and open rates are easy to report and easy to misread. For a brokerage, these numbers say more about whether marketing is working:


Metric Why it matters


Proposal-to-bind rate The cleanest read on whether the client-facing work persuades. Track it by producer and by line.


Time from quote to proposal Speed wins accounts. A proposal that lands the same day the quotes arrive beats one that lands next week.


Retention rate Keeping a client costs less than winning a new one, and a small retention gain compounds every year.


Policies per client The direct result of cross-sell campaigns to your own book.


Review volume and rating by office Feeds local search and referral trust, and shows where service needs help.


AI answer mentions How often ChatGPT and Google AI answers name your agency for the lines you write.


## Mistakes to avoid with AI in insurance marketing


- **Publishing coverage claims nobody reviewed.** AI can draft an article about business interruption coverage. A licensed person should read it before it goes live. A wrong coverage statement is an E&O issue, not a typo.
- **Ignoring advertising and consent rules.** Insurance advertising rules vary by state, and text campaigns need documented consent. Check both before you automate outreach.
- **Buying a suite to fix one problem.** Adopt one tool per measured bottleneck. Unused modules cost money and attention.
- **Leaving the proposal out of the brand.** If the website looks premium and the proposal looks homemade, clients believe the proposal.
- **Sending client data to tools that train on it.** Ask every vendor about model training, retention, and access controls. CopyCat never uses customer documents to train AI models and holds a SOC 2 Type II report.


## Frequently asked questions


### What are the best AI tools for insurance agency marketing?


Pick one tool per job: CopyCat for the proposals, one-pagers, email summaries, and comparisons every client sees; HubSpot for CRM and automation; Agency Revolution or AgencyZoom for insurance-specific campaigns; Canva for design; Semrush for SEO and AI search; Birdeye for reviews; Circleback for meeting insights; Descript for video; and Clay for commercial prospect research.


### How can an insurance brokerage improve its marketing?


Start with the documents clients read. Lock the brand into proposal and renewal templates, send a summary with every proposal, market to your own book by line of business, answer buyer questions so AI search can cite you, build a review program, and measure proposal-to-bind rate and retention.


### Why should the marketing team own the proposal?


It is the most-read marketing asset the agency produces, and it is read at the moment of decision. When every producer builds it their own way, the brand the client sees depends on who quoted them.


### How do larger agencies keep proposals consistent across producers?


Put the brand in the template, not a style guide. In CopyCat every producer builds from the same agency templates on a shared board, changes are logged, and the analytics dashboard shows activity across the team.


### Can AI write insurance marketing content on its own?


Use it for drafts, research, and repurposing. Keep a licensed reviewer on anything that describes coverage, and check state advertising rules and consent requirements before automating outreach.
